newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK OPPOSITION FAILS TO OUST INTERIOR MINISTER.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK OPPOSITION FAILS TO OUST INTERIOR MINISTER.

text.p: Slovak opposition deputies failed on Thursday in a bid to oust Interior Minister Gustav Krajci for his role in last month's chaos surrounding a constitutional referendum, unable to muster a quorum.

Thursday's extraordinary parliamentary session had been convened by the opposition with the only agenda item being a vote of no-confidence in Krajci for single-handedly stripping a question on direct presidential elections from the ballot.

The ruling parliamentary opposition parties -- the Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, the ultra-right Slovak National Party (SNS) and the ultra-left Workers' Party (ZRS) - boycotted the session and the neccessary 76 deputies out of 150 could not be mustered.

The opposition claimed that Krajci had acted illegally by omitting a question on direct presidential elections from the original ballot paper which contained three questions on Slovakia's willingness to join NATO.
Krajci, who was present at Thursday's session, interpreted a Constitutional Court ruling as meaning that the presidential question was unconstitutional.
However court officials said Krajci's interpretation of the was incorrect and that the question on the direct election of the president should have been included on the ballot.
Some 90 percent of Slovakia's eligible voters either failed to turn out for the referendum or refused to vote with the ballots containing only the NATO questions.
The fiasco has been widely criticised by Slovaks and foreign observers.

Direct presidential elections are seen by the opposition as the only way of solving a potential constitutional crisis early next year when President Michal Kovac, Meciar's political arch-enemy, steps down at the end of his term at the beginning of March.
In its present composition parliament would probably be unable to agree on a candidate who would get the necessary three-fifths majority of votes needed to elect a new president.
In this case most presidential powers would revert to the government, effectively to Meciar, which the opposition wants to prevent.
